Now, let’s look
behind the interface
My contribution: backend architecture and engineering
I built the services that validate requests, protect data, run background work and support real-time chat.

My teammates have presented the product and their contributions. Now I am going to take you behind the interface and explain what happens in the backend. My name is Mohammed Elmahfoudi, the backend guy on the team. I was responsible for the server-side architecture and implementation.
The same backend serves candidates, company teams and platform administrators.
Offers, candidate review and hiring stages
Users, companies, support and audit activity
Validate requests, enforce access rules, preserve data and coordinate external services.

The backend has 165 routes across 18 routers, supported by 29 database models and 46 migrations. Its 53 test files contain 372 test functions covering security and business workflows. These components serve candidates, company teams and administrators.
FastAPI separates immediate requests, durable background work and real-time delivery.

Normal requests pass through Nginx and FastAPI to PostgreSQL. Background jobs use an outbox, Redis and Celery. WebSockets use short-lived tickets, PostgreSQL history and Redis fan-out. Inside the code, routers receive input, dependencies load identity, services make decisions, models protect state and workers handle slow operations.
Validation, authentication and authorization happen before business logic.
Approved Origin plus matching CSRF cookie and X-CSRF-Token header.
Expected errors remain explicit. Unexpected failures return a safe message and traceable error ID.

A request first matches a route and passes Pydantic validation. The backend then resolves the current session and checks role, company, ownership and resource scope. Only then does it run service logic and commit the transaction. Cookie mutations also require CSRF protection.
Application is the central record linking the candidate, offer, CV, screening and interviews.

status and stage_version
AI screening result
interview schedule and notes

The Application model connects one candidate to one offer and preserves the recruitment workflow. The database prevents duplicate applications and verifies CV ownership. Under concurrency, row locks, version checks, unique constraints and idempotency keep state correct.
A token identifies a session. Current user state and resource ownership decide authority.
Can this type of user perform the action?
Does the record belong to this user or company?
Otherwise return a safe 403 or 404 response.
2FA challenges are short-lived and single use. Redis rejects revoked sessions quickly; PostgreSQL remains the durable source of truth.

Registration uses email verification and login uses bcrypt. Sessions use JWTs and secure cookies, but every protected request still loads current user state. Authorization combines role permission with tenant or ownership scope. Two-factor challenges are single-use and sessions remain revocable.
The backend guards every recruitment stage and records the history.
Before commit: current stage + requested stage + caller permission + application scope

A candidate discovers an offer and applies with a valid profile and CV. The backend creates AI screening work, allows company review, manages interview feedback and controls the final decision. Every transition checks the current stage, requested stage, caller permission and application scope.
Durable AI jobs and email delivery
Slow external services run outside the HTTP request and remain safe to retry.
PostgreSQL preserves pending work. Bounded retry, leases and idempotency prevent loss and duplicate effects.

AI work first becomes a durable database job, then a dispatcher and Celery worker process it through Redis. Email uses the same outbox idea with encrypted payloads, deduplication and provider idempotency. Both workflows survive restarts and temporary provider failures.
Three production boundaries protect live communication, sensitive assets and infrastructure.
Recruitment chat scoped to an application
Validate file type, size and owner
Store CVs in private Supabase buckets
Authorize every download through the API
Nginx is the only public entry point
API, database, Redis and workers stay private
WebSocket access, file downloads and internal services all rely on server-side authorization rather than client trust.

The recruitment and friend WebSockets both use short-lived tickets and durable PostgreSQL history. CVs stay in private storage and every download passes through authorization. In production, Nginx is the only public entry point while data stores and workers remain private.
The backend combines automated evidence with one connected workflow for the live demonstration.
Tokens do not replace role and scope checks
Next: load testing, distributed tracing, job dashboards and query profiling

The repository contains 53 test files and 372 test functions covering the main security and workflow risks. My main lessons were that current state controls authority, database rules support security and slow work needs durability. My next improvements are load testing, distributed tracing, job dashboards and query profiling. Thank you, and I am ready for your questions.
